title: The 86% habit of couples who last
lines: One tiny habit predicted which newlyweds would *still be together* six years later.
Psychologist John Gottman watched couples spend a weekend in a lab apartment.
He was waiting for moments like this: one partner says, *look at that bird.*
That's a bid. A small request for attention.
The couples who stayed married turned toward those bids *86 percent* of the time.
The couples who divorced? *33 percent.*
Not the big fights. Not the anniversaries.
Just whether you look up when they point at the bird.
So next time they say *look at this*... look.

title: What holding hands does to your brain
lines: Holding hands changes what your brain does with *fear*.
Researchers put married women in a brain scanner and told them a small shock might come.
Then they tried it three ways: no hand, a stranger's hand, or their *husband's* hand.
With their husband, the brain's threat response dropped *the most*.
And the happier the marriage, the *calmer* the brain stayed.
A stranger's hand helped a little. The person they trusted helped far more.
So when your partner is nervous before something big, skip the pep talk.
Just *hold their hand*.

title: Do couples really start to look alike?
lines: Couples who've been together for decades start to *look alike*. Right?
A famous 1987 study said yes. So Stanford researchers checked again.
They gathered photos of *517 couples*, taken early on and again 20 to 69 years later.
Both people and a face-recognition algorithm compared them.
The result: couples did *not* grow more alike over time.
They already looked similar *from the very start*.
So we don't turn into our partner's twin.
We just tend to pick someone who looks a bit like us.
Be honest... does yours?
